newsitem.title: ITALY: Britons tell of nightmare night on Albanian beach.
newsitem.headline: Britons tell of nightmare night on Albanian beach.

text.p: Several Britons rescued from Albania complained on Friday that the crack Italian soldiers sent to get them had abandoned them overnight on a freezing beach at the mercy of an armed mob.

Some of the Britons, ferried to southern Italy on the warship San Giusto, reported on their arrival in Brindisi that the Italians had shot dead one Albanian man and wounded four in a gun battle in the port of Durres on Thursday night.

They said the Italians, who rescued around 900 people of various nationalities between Thursday evening and early Friday, then retreated out to sea and did not return until after dawn to pick them up, leaving them in a nightmare situation.
"You've got to ask the Italian authorities why they evacuated their own people and left women and children on the beach to face a wild mob firing Kalashnikovs," oil worker Derek Tyldsey told Reuters.
"They (the Italians) were firing over our heads. It was terrifying and then they just left us," said a missionary teacher who did not give her name.

The Italian Defence Ministry said earlier that the operation, involving around 100 fusiliers from the crack San Marco Battalion, had been suspended for several hours overnight due to shooting in the air by Albanians and fog.
It made no mention of any casualties.
"It was an emergency evacuation, not a stroll," an Italian official said of the operation after the Britons' complaints.
Britain and the United States have congratulated Italy for rescuing their nationals, who were among some 900 evacuees on the San Giusto when it docked in the port of Brindisi.
A British Foreign Office statement expressed Britain's "delight" at the success of the evacuation.

"The Italian forces behaved impeccably in very dangerous circumstances. We asked them to get the British out safe and well and this is what they did," senior diplomat Keith Bloomfield, from the British embassy in Rome, said in Brindisi.
Molly Bicker, the wife of the British vice-consul in Albania, said: "the Albanians were very menacing until Croat oil men drew their cars up around us in a defensive semi circle."
She added that it had been cold but she had never doubted that the Italians would return to collect them.
Some of the other foreigners, who set out for Durres from the capital Tirana by car in an evacuation organised by the British embassy there, sounded more shaken.
"Albanians were trying to force their way on to the landing craft and I think the Italians panicked," said Baptist missionary Paul Towlson.
"They began shooting over their (the Albanians') heads and the crowd rushed back and trampled some of us.
"An Italian stun grenade exploded just a couple of feet from us, it was very frightening. I don't think that the Italians realised that we were all behind the Albanians."
Towlson said he saw one Albanian fall and then be dragged off by a friend.

"We were told he'd been shot in the back and it's easy to believe he could have been killed but there was no way of checking this," he said, adding that the Italians had retreated with their landing craft half empty.
"We expected them to come straight back but it took them six and a half hours," he added.
Ernesto Pullano, the captain of the San Giorgio, said he was delighted with the operation. "It all went well and the praise goes to all those who took part," he said.
